lesson.title: From Bare Ground to Forest: How Communities Change Through Time
lesson.summary: Ecological succession is the gradual, somewhat predictable process by which the species composition of a community changes over time, typically progressing from a small number of hardy early colonizing species toward a more complex, diverse community.
lesson.body:
Everything covered so far in this unit, competition, mutualism, commensalism, parasitism, keystone species, and trophic cascades, describes interactions within a community at essentially one point in time. Ecological succession zooms out and asks a different question: how does the whole community change over longer stretches of time, sometimes years, sometimes centuries? Succession is the process by which the mix of species living in a given area shifts in a somewhat orderly sequence, usually starting with a small number of hardy species that can tolerate difficult conditions and gradually building toward a more diverse, more complex community as conditions change.

Early ecologists sometimes described succession as ending in a stable, self perpetuating climax community, a final, settled stage that would persist indefinitely unless disturbed again. That idea remains useful as a rough description, but modern ecologists treat it with real caution. Real communities are shaped by chance events, local variation in soil, climate, and species availability, and disturbances of all sizes, so what actually develops in a given place is often more open ended, and slower to settle into any single fixed endpoint, than the classic climax model suggested. Succession is better thought of as a general, directional trend, from few species to more, from short lived colonizers to longer lived and more competitively dominant species, rather than a rigid, guaranteed march toward one predetermined final community.

Ecologists divide succession into two broad categories based on the starting point. Primary succession begins on bare substrate that has no soil at all, such as newly exposed rock after a glacier retreats or fresh volcanic rock after an eruption, and it has to start essentially from scratch, including the very slow process of building soil itself. Secondary succession begins in a place where soil already exists but the community has been disturbed or removed, such as after a wildfire burns through a forest or after farmland is abandoned, and because soil, and often a bank of seeds and roots, is already present, secondary succession typically proceeds much faster than primary succession. The next two chapters look at each of these in turn, starting with primary succession, the slower and more dramatic case of building a community from bare ground up.
